templates.pattern: A block of mass [M] kg of a material with specific heat capacity [C] J/kg°C is heated and its temperature rises by [DT]°C. Calculate the energy absorbed by the block in joules.
templates.explanation:
Energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
= mcΔT
= [M] × [C] × [DT]
= [RESULT] J

Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1°C. Water has a very high SHC of 4200 J/kg°C.

templates.pattern: An electric heater supplies [Q] J of energy to [M] kg of a substance and its temperature rises by [DT]°C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of the substance in J/kg°C.
templates.explanation:
Specific Heat Capacity c = Q ÷ (m × ΔT)
= [Q] ÷ ([M] × [DT])
= [Q] ÷ [M*DT]
= [RESULT] J/kg°C

This is how specific heat capacity is measured experimentally using an electric heater.

templates.pattern: A current of [I] A flows through a component connected to a [V] V supply for [T] seconds. Calculate the electrical energy transferred in joules.
templates.explanation:
Electrical Energy = Voltage × Current × Time
= V × I × t
= [V] × [I] × [T]
= [RESULT] J

This formula combines Ohm's law and the definition of power to give total energy transferred.

templates.pattern: A component is connected to a [V] V supply and draws a current of [I] A. Calculate the electrical power consumed by the component in watts.
templates.explanation:
Electrical Power = Voltage × Current
= P = VI
= [V] × [I]
= [RESULT] W

This is one of the most important equations in electricity. It applies to any electrical component.

templates.pattern: A resistor of resistance [R] Ω carries a current of [I] A. Calculate the power dissipated by the resistor in watts.
templates.explanation:
Power = I² × R
= [I]² × [R]
= [I*I] × [R]
= [RESULT] W

This shows why high currents cause large power losses. Doubling the current quadruples the power dissipated as heat.

templates.pattern: A resistor of resistance [R] Ω is connected across a [V] V supply. Calculate the power dissipated by the resistor in watts.
templates.explanation:
Power = V² ÷ R
= [V]² ÷ [R]
= [V*V] ÷ [R]
= [RESULT] W

This formula is useful when you know the voltage but not the current. It is derived by combining P = VI with V = IR.

templates.pattern: An object of mass [M] kg slides down a slope from a height of [H] m and reaches the bottom with a velocity of [V] m/s. Calculate the energy lost to friction in joules. (g = 10 m/s²)
templates.explanation:
Energy lost to friction = GPE at top − KE at bottom
= mgh − ½mv²
= ([M] × 10 × [H]) − (0.5 × [M] × [V]²)
= [M*10*H] − [0.5*M*V*V]
= [RESULT] J

In a real situation not all GPE converts to KE — some is lost as heat through friction.

templates.pattern: A spring with spring constant [K] N/m is compressed by [X] m from its natural length. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the spring in joules.
templates.explanation:
Elastic Potential Energy = ½ × spring constant × extension²
= ½kx²
= 0.5 × [K] × [X]²
= 0.5 × [K] × [X*X]
= [RESULT] J

The spring constant k measures the stiffness of the spring. A stiffer spring stores more energy for the same compression.

templates.pattern: A pump of efficiency [EFF]% raises [M] kg of water to a height of [H] m in [T] seconds. Calculate the electrical power input to the pump in watts. (g = 10 m/s²)
templates.explanation:
Useful power = mgh ÷ t
= ([M] × 10 × [H]) ÷ [T] W

Power input = Useful power × 100 ÷ efficiency
= [M*10*H/T] × 100 ÷ [EFF]
= [RESULT] W

Because the pump is not 100% efficient it needs more electrical power than the useful output.

templates.pattern: A household uses [KWH] kWh of electricity. The cost of electricity is [PRICE] pence per kWh. Calculate the total cost in pence.
templates.explanation:
Total cost = energy used × cost per unit
= [KWH] × [PRICE]
= [RESULT] pence

To convert to pounds divide by 100. Energy companies charge per kilowatt-hour — this is why energy efficiency saves money.
